tagline.text: A Bohol landscape where a thousand green hills turn brown

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: February–May (dry season, when the hills turn brown)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–3,500 per person (including a countryside tour)

children.text: A signature Philippine landscape of 1,200 to 1,700-odd cone-shaped limestone hills rising across about 50 km² in the middle of Bohol Island. In the dry season, the grass dries out and the hills turn chocolate-brown; a viewpoint and ATV rides let you experience them up close.

The Chocolate Hills are a cluster of cone-shaped hills scattered across Carmen, Batuan, and Sagbayan in central Bohol. Depending on the counting method, the hills number anywhere from 1,268 to 1,776, rising across about 50 km², mostly
tall, with the highest exceeding

. They look as if someone had scattered giant chocolate kisses across the grassland, and this signature Philippine scene appears without fail on the back of the 200-peso bill and in tourism promotions.

The hills are explained as karst terrain: coral reef and limestone that piled up on an ancient seabed were later uplifted, and over long ages, rain and groundwater eroded them until only the hardest parts remained as cones. Almost no trees grow on the hills, only grass, so they're green in the rainy season but turn brown when the grass dries out in the dry season — the source of the "chocolate" name. Local legend also tells of boulders thrown by two feuding giants, or of hardened tears shed by a giant named Arogo over an unrequited love.
The Chocolate Hills were designated a National Geological Monument in
, and when the whole of Bohol Island was recognized in
as the Philippines' first UNESCO Global Geopark (the Bohol Island Geopark), they became its centerpiece attraction. In
, a resort built among the hills drew nationwide attention over a protected-area controversy.

The visit itself centers on climbing to the viewpoint for the view, so an hour or two is enough, but most travelers combine it into a "countryside tour" for the day along with the Tarsier Sanctuary, the Loboc River cruise, and Baclayon Church. It's a must on the itinerary for families with children, a filial trip with parents, or anyone visiting Bohol for the first time.
About 214 steps cut into one of the hills at the Chocolate Hills Complex take you up to a view of hills stretching endlessly in every direction. The stairs are steep but climbable in about
10 minutes

blocks.title: Riding an ATV between the hills

children.text: ATV operators near the viewpoint run courses along dirt paths between the hills. A
30-minute to 1-hour
course is typical, and since mud gets splattered, wear clothes you don't mind getting dirty.
At the Adventure Park (CHAP), about
10 minutes
toward Bilar, you can enjoy a bike zipline and rope course crossing over the hills, as well as a regular zipline.

blocks.title: A different angle from Sagbayan Peak

children.text: Sagbayan Peak to the north is smaller in scale but less crowded, with restaurants and play areas, making it good for families.

blocks.title: Drive through the Bilar mahogany forest

children.text: On the road from Tagbilaran to the Chocolate Hills, Bilar has about
2km
of densely planted mahogany trees forming a man-made forest — a good spot to pull over briefly for photos.

blocks.title: Combine it into a countryside tour

children.text: It's most efficient to see the Blood Compact Shrine, Baclayon Church, the Tarsier Sanctuary, and the Loboc River lunch cruise together with the Chocolate Hills in a single day.
Near closing time, the low sun casts long shadows across each hill, producing more three-dimensional photos than at midday.

It takes about
1 hour 20 minutes

from Manila to Bohol–Panglao International Airport (TAG), with daily flights from Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific, and others. Direct flights from Incheon, Korea, to Bohol also operate, though this varies by airline and season. From the airport to the Chocolate Hills is about
1.5–2 hours
by car.
Fast craft such as OceanJet run several times daily from Cebu to Tagbilaran Port; the trip takes about
2 hours
, with fares of about
depending on seat class.
A bus to Carmen from the Dao Integrated Bus Terminal in Tagbilaran takes about
1.5–2 hours
, with a fare of about
. Ask to be let off on the road at the viewpoint entrance; from there, an uphill road leads to the viewpoint, so it's easier to take a habal-habal (about
). Return buses become less frequent later in the afternoon.
The most comfortable option is to charter a van or car for the day and do the countryside tour. Starting from Panglao, a car runs about
, with entrance fees and meals usually extra. Many travelers rent their own motorbike, but it's a one-way mountain drive of about
60km
, so you should have riding experience.
The hills take on their namesake chocolate color mainly during the drier
late February to May
April–May
especially sees the grass dry out the most for a deep brown, but midday temperatures can top 33°C, so an early-morning visit is best.
June–January
is the rainy season and its aftermath, when the hills stay green — the green hills have their own beauty, and the clear air makes for sharp photos.
Bohol sits on the southern edge of the Philippine typhoon path, so it's less affected than Luzon, but
October–December
can bring low-pressure systems and heavy rain that make mountain roads slippery and turn the ATV course muddy. Around the third week of
July
, when the Sandugo Festival is held across Bohol, Tagbilaran gets crowded.

and may vary depending on local conditions.
Since the Chocolate Hills are usually a day trip, accommodation is generally booked on Panglao Island (around Alona Beach) or in Tagbilaran city. Beachfront resorts on Panglao run about
or more a night, and Tagbilaran city hotels run about
. If you want quiet countryside scenery, another option is to spend a night at a riverside or mountain lodge near Loboc or Bilar and see the Chocolate Hills early the next morning.

Near the viewpoint there are souvenir shops and a few simple restaurants, but options are limited, so many countryside tours handle lunch with the Loboc River cruise buffet. Bohol specialty snacks such as calamay (a chewy rice cake served in coconut husks), ube (purple yam) desserts, and piaya are popular souvenirs to buy.
It's best to assume there's no ATM near the viewpoint. Prepare cash for entrance fees, the ATV, and snacks.
Arriving around
lets you climb the stairs before the tour groups arrive. There's almost no shade at midday, and it gets very hot.
It's windy at the top of the viewpoint, so wear a hat with a strap, and check on-site rules before flying a drone.
ATV operators vary in course and duration, so confirm and negotiate "how many minutes to which viewpoint" — most include photo stops.
When booking a countryside tour, be sure to confirm whether the entrance fee and the Loboc cruise are included, and the pickup time.
Phone signal generally reaches near the viewpoint but is weak through the Bilar forest section.
Popular photo compositions are looking down at the hills from partway up the stairs, and the rice paddies beyond the hills along the ATV course.
Climbing onto the hills or digging into their soil violates protected-area rules. Do not leave the viewpoint or the designated ATV course.
The viewpoint stairs are steep and slippery when wet. Anyone with weak knees should climb slowly and hold the railing.
ATVs occasionally roll over. Wear a helmet, follow behind the guide, and have children ride in a car with a guide.
Entrance fees and operating rules have changed under municipal ordinances over time. Check the latest notices from the Carmen municipal government or the Bohol tourism office before visiting.
Midday sun is very strong, so be sure to bring water, sunscreen, and a hat.
